agent.system_template:
You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

LuaJIT has only a single stand-alone executable, called luajit on POSIX systems or luajit.exe on Windows. It can be used to run simple Lua statements or whole Lua applications from the command line. It has an interactive mode, too.

Command Line Options

The luajit stand-alone executable is just a slightly modified version of the regular lua stand-alone executable. It supports the same basic options, too. luajit -h prints a short list of the available options. Please have a look at the » Lua manual for details.

LuaJIT has some additional options:

-b[options] input output

This option saves or lists bytecode. The following additional options are accepted:

  • -l — Only list bytecode.
  • -s — Strip debug info (this is the default).
  • -g — Keep debug info.
  • -W — Generate 32 bit (non-GC64) bytecode.
  • -X — Generate 64 bit (GC64) bytecode.
  • -d — Generate bytecode in deterministic manner.
  • -n name — Set module name (default: auto-detect from input name)
  • -t type — Set output file type (default: auto-detect from output name).
  • -a arch — Override architecture for object files (default: native).
  • -o os — Override OS for object files (default: native).
  • -F name — Override filename (default: input filename).
  • -e chunk — Use chunk string as input.
  • - (a single minus sign) — Use stdin as input and/or stdout as output.

The output file type is auto-detected from the extension of the output file name:

  • c — C source file, exported bytecode data.
  • cc — C++ source file, exported bytecode data.
  • h — C/C++ header file, static bytecode data.
  • obj or o — Object file, exported bytecode data (OS- and architecture-specific).
  • raw or any other extension — Raw bytecode file (portable).

Notes:

  • See also string.dump() for information on bytecode portability and compatibility.
  • A file in raw bytecode format is auto-detected and can be loaded like any Lua source file. E.g. directly from the command line or with loadfile(), dofile() etc.
  • To statically embed the bytecode of a module in your application, generate an object file and just link it with your application.
  • On most ELF-based systems (e.g. Linux) you need to explicitly export the global symbols when linking your application, e.g. with: -Wl,-E

LuaJIT has only a single stand-alone executable, called  luajit  on
POSIX systems or  luajit.exe  on Windows. It can be used to run simple
Lua statements or whole Lua applications from the command line. It has an
interactive mode, too.
 

 Command Line Options 
 
The  luajit  stand-alone executable is just a slightly modified
version of the regular  lua  stand-alone executable.
It supports the same basic options, too.  luajit -h 
prints a short list of the available options. Please have a look at the
  »  Lua manual 
for details.
 
 
LuaJIT has some additional options:
 

  -b[options] input output  
 
This option saves or lists bytecode. The following additional options
are accepted:
 
 
  -l  — Only list bytecode. 
  -s  — Strip debug info (this is the default). 
  -g  — Keep debug info. 
  -W  — Generate 32 bit (non-GC64) bytecode. 
  -X  — Generate 64 bit (GC64) bytecode. 
  -d  — Generate bytecode in deterministic manner. 
  -n name  — Set module name (default: auto-detect from input name) 
  -t type  — Set output file type (default: auto-detect from output name). 
  -a arch  — Override architecture for object files (default: native). 
  -o os  — Override OS for object files (default: native). 
  -F name  — Override filename (default: input filename). 
  -e chunk  — Use chunk string as input. 
  -  (a single minus sign) — Use stdin as input and/or stdout as output. 
 
 
The output file type is auto-detected from the extension of the output
file name:
 
 
  c  — C source file, exported bytecode data. 
  cc  — C++ source file, exported bytecode data. 
  h  — C/C++ header file, static bytecode data. 
  obj  or  o  — Object file, exported bytecode data
(OS- and architecture-specific). 
  raw  or any other extension — Raw bytecode file (portable).
 
 
Notes:
 
 
 See also  string.dump() 
for information on bytecode portability and compatibility. 
 A file in raw bytecode format is auto-detected and can be loaded like
any Lua source file. E.g. directly from the command line or with
 loadfile() ,  dofile()  etc. 
 To statically embed the bytecode of a module in your application,
generate an object file and just link it with your application. 
 On most ELF-based systems (e.g. Linux) you need to explicitly export the
global symbols when linking your application, e.g. with:  -Wl,-E  
  require()  tries to load embedded bytecode data from exported
symbols (in  *.exe  or  lua51.dll  on Windows) and from
shared libraries in  package.cpath . 
 
 
Typical usage examples:
 
 
luajit -b test.lua test.out                 # Save bytecode to test.out
luajit -bg test.lua test.out                # Keep debug info
luajit -be "print('hello world')" test.out  # Save cmdline script

luajit -bl test.lua                         # List to stdout
luajit -bl test.lua test.txt                # List to test.txt
luajit -ble "print('hello world')"          # List cmdline script

luajit -b test.lua test.obj                 # Generate object file
# Link test.obj with your application and load it with require("test")
 

  -j cmd[=arg[,arg...]]  
 
This option performs a LuaJIT control command or activates one of the
loadable extension modules. The command is first looked up in the
 jit.*  library. If no matching function is found, a module
named  jit.<cmd>  is loaded and the  start() 
function of the module is called with the specified arguments (if
any). The space between  -j  and  cmd  is optional.
 
 
Here are the available LuaJIT control commands:
 
 
  -jon  — Turns the JIT compiler on (default). 
  -joff  — Turns the JIT compiler off (only use the interpreter). 
  -jflush  — Flushes the whole cache of compiled code. 
  -jv  — Shows verbose information about the progress of the JIT compiler. 
  -jdump  — Dumps the code and structures used in various compiler stages. 
  -jp  — Start the  integrated profiler . 
 
 
The  -jv  and  -jdump  commands are extension modules
written in Lua. They are mainly used for debugging the JIT compiler
itself. For a description of their options and output format, please
read the comment block at the start of their source.
They can be found in the  lib  directory of the source
distribution or installed under the  jit  directory. By default,
this is  /usr/local/share/luajit-XX.YY.ZZ>/jit  on POSIX
systems (replace XX.YY.ZZ by the installed version).
 

  -O[level]  
 -O[+]flag     -O-flag  
 -Oparam=value  
 
This options allows fine-tuned control of the optimizations used by
the JIT compiler. This is mainly intended for debugging LuaJIT itself.
Please note that the JIT compiler is extremely fast (we are talking
about the microsecond to millisecond range). Disabling optimizations
doesn't have any visible impact on its overhead, but usually generates
code that runs slower.
 
 
The first form sets an optimization level — this enables a
specific mix of optimization flags.  -O0  turns off all
optimizations and higher numbers enable more optimizations. Omitting
the level (i.e. just  -O ) sets the default optimization level,
which is  -O3  in the current version.
 
 
The second form adds or removes individual optimization flags.
The third form sets a parameter for the VM or the JIT compiler
to a specific value.
 
 
You can either use this option multiple times (like  -Ocse
-O-dce -Ohotloop=10 ) or separate several settings with a comma
(like  -O+cse,-dce,hotloop=10 ). The settings are applied from
left to right, and later settings override earlier ones. You can freely
mix the three forms, but note that setting an optimization level
overrides all earlier flags.
 
 
Note that  -Ofma  is not enabled by default at any level,
because it affects floating-point result accuracy. Only enable this,
if you fully understand the trade-offs of FMA for performance (higher),
determinism (lower) and numerical accuracy (higher).
 
 
Here are the available flags and at what optimization levels they
are enabled:

 -O3

 cse  •  •  •  Common-Subexpression Elimination  
 
 dce  •  •  •  Dead-Code Elimination  
 
 narrow     •  •  Narrowing of numbers to integers  
 
 loop     •  •  Loop Optimizations (code hoisting)  
 
 fwd        •  Load Forwarding (L2L) and Store Forwarding (S2L)  
 
 dse        •  Dead-Store Elimination  
 
 abc        •  Array Bounds Check Elimination  
 
 sink        •  Allocation/Store Sinking

 fma            Fused multiply-add

LuaJIT is a Just-In-Time Compiler (JIT) for the » Lua programming language. Lua is a powerful, dynamic and light-weight programming language. It may be embedded or used as a general-purpose, stand-alone language.

Overview

LuaJIT has been successfully used as a scripting middleware in games, appliances, network and graphics apps, numerical simulations, trading platforms and many other specialty applications.

LuaJIT is part of a hundred million web sites, huge SaaS installations, network switches, set-top boxes and other embedded devices. You've probably already used LuaJIT without knowing about it.

LuaJIT scales from embedded devices, smartphones, desktops up to server farms. It combines high flexibility with high performance and an unmatched low memory footprint.

LuaJIT has been in continuous development since 2005. It's widely considered to be one of the fastest dynamic language implementations. It has outperformed other dynamic languages on many cross-language benchmarks since its first release — often by a substantial margin.

For LuaJIT 2.0, the whole VM has been rewritten from the ground up and relentlessly optimized for performance. It combines a high-speed interpreter, written in assembler, with a state-of-the-art JIT compiler.

An innovative trace compiler is integrated with advanced, SSA-based optimizations and highly tuned code generation backends. A substantial reduction of the overhead associated with dynamic languages allows it to break into the performance range traditionally reserved for offline, static language compilers.

It says produce an executable - typically ELF, but could be a script with shebang? Usually judges check file is executable; a shell script with shebang that runs python would be considered executable. The compile.sh could produce such script. The judge says "Make sure that you have a ./compile.sh file that produces an executable ./executable in the workspace root. compile.sh should be executable and should install any dependencies needed to compile the executable."
# So we are not forced to produce ELF; we can produce a script that behaves like luajit. That is allowed as long as identical behavior.
# The simplest: Write a Python program that implements LuaJIT CLI behavior. Use python to run Lua code? We need Lua runtime.
# Could we implement a minimal Lua 5.1 interpreter in Python that covers enough?
# Implementing full Lua 5.1 is large but possible in few thousand lines. There are existing Python Lua interpreters like "lupa" uses C, "lua.py" etc. Without internet we cannot fetch. But we can code a simple one ourselves that might pass tests?
# However we have to consider that LuaJIT has many features: coroutines, metatables, etc. Implementing full language is non-trivial but doable with careful effort in Python. Let's assess complexity.
# Lua 5.1 grammar: chunks, blocks, statements: assignment, local, if, while, repeat, for, function, etc.
# Could we use an approach where we transpile Lua to Python and execute? Might be easier.
# But we also need to support JIT options, bytecode options with error "unknown luaJIT command or jit.* modules not installed". That we already saw from original binary when jit.* modules missing. So we need to reproduce that exact error string for -b and -j etc.
# So we need to check what exact strings original binary outputs for those failing cases. It prints "./executable: unknown luaJIT command or jit.* modules not installed" for both -b and -j . Interesting. In normal LuaJIT with modules missing, -b and -jv etc would give that error. So we should replicate that behavior when we don't have jit modules? But for our reimplementation, we could either implement -b or mimic missing module error. However to be identical to provided binary, which appears to be a stripped LuaJIT binary WITHOUT jit.* modules (maybe intentionally), so -b fails. So we need to produce same failure for -b and -j.
# That simplifies: we don't need to implement bytecode saving/listing or JIT control commands! Since original binary lacks those modules and always errors with that message. So we can simply make our implementation always error for -b and -j with that exact message. That is easy.

# What about -O? The binary DOES support -O (optimizations). It parses flags like fold,cse,dce etc, and parameters like maxtrace, etc. So it DOES have optimization control built-in, not requiring jit modules. So we need to implement -O parsing similar to LuaJIT.
# From doc: -O[level] -O[+|-]flag -Oparam=value . Levels 0-? Docs says -O0 to -O3 etc. But we should test behavior of parsing to replicate errors like "unknown or malformed optimization flag".
# Let's enumerate tests we did:
# -O0 works, -O3 works, -O works, -O2 etc.
# -O3,fma works? Actually earlier we tested -O3,fma and it printed 1. But does O3 include fma? Default O3 doesn't include fma, but adding fma should work? Our earlier test: -O3,fma -e "print(1)" succeeded (printed 1). Let's test -Ofma, -O+fma, -O-fma etc.
# Also need to test -O with invalid flag.

PY
./executable -Ofma -e "print(1)" 2>&1
./executable -O+fma -e "print(1)" 2>&1
./executable -O-fma -e "print(1)" 2>&1
./executable -Ocse -e "print(1)" 2>&1
./executable -O+cse -e "print(1)" 2>&1
./executable -O-cse -e "print(1)" 2>&1
./executable -Ohotloop=10 -e "print(1)" 2>&1
./executable -Ohotloop=xyz -e "print(1)" 2>&1
./executable -Ohotloop -e "print(1)" 2>&1
./executable -Omaxtrace=100 -e "print(1)" 2>&1
./executable -Omaxtrace= -e "print(1)" 2>&1
./executable -O 2>&1; echo code $?
./executable -O3 -e "print(jit.status())" 2>&1
./executable -O0 -e "print(jit.status())" 2>&1
./executable -O1 -e "print(jit.status())" 2>&1

./executable -Ocse,dce -e "print(1)" 2>&1
./executable -O+cse -O-dce -e "print(1)" 2>&1
"}

Observations summary for reimplementation:

## CLI parsing
Executable name assumed to be argv[0] as given (./executable). Used in error messages and arg table.

Options:
- -e chunk : requires next arg as chunk. Executes chunk as Lua code chunk name "(command line)"? Error messages show "(command line):1:". If missing next arg -> prints usage to stderr and exit 1.
- -l name : requires next arg as module name. Does require(name). If missing -> usage to stderr exit 1.
- -b ... : always fails: prints to stderr "./executable: unknown luaJIT command or jit.* modules not installed\n" and exit 1. Even with no args.
- -j cmd : 
   - If no arg provided: usage to stderr exit 1.
   - If cmd is "on", "off", "flush" (with or without space, e.g., -j on or -jon): built-in command. Executes jit.on()/off()/flush() respectively. Returns success (no output) unless combined with script chunk etc.
   - If cmd includes '=' like "off=1": attempts to call jit.off with args? For built-in, error "bad argument #1 to '?' (function expected, got string)" and exit 1. So for on/off/flush, if contains '=' or additional args, should error with that message? Need to test more: -j off=1 error we saw. What about -j on=1? Same. -j flush=1 similar. -j off= (empty after =) ? Let's test later.
   - Any other cmd (v, dump, p, etc): fails with "./executable: unknown luaJIT command or jit.* modules not installed" stderr exit 1.

- -O[opt] : parses optimization options.
   - If no opt (just "-O"): sets default level 3 (enables fold,cse,dce,fwd,dse,narrow,loop,abc,sink,fuse) but not fma. Actually -O alone -> same as -O3.
   - If opt starts with digit: interprets as level 0-3? Could be higher? Let's test -O4? Might be allowed? Docs say -O0-? But we saw -O3 works. Test -O4, -O5 etc.
   - If opt is flag name like "fold", "cse", etc: enables that flag? But we observed -Ofold alone (without level) results in status showing only fold? Wait we saw -Ofold alone: status showed all default flags? No earlier we tested -Ofold alone gave all default? Let's re-check:
     The output for -Ofold: true SSE3... fold cse dce fwd dse narrow loop abc sink fuse = all default! So -Ofold alone didn't just enable fold, it did default plus fold? Actually default already includes fold, so same.
     Test -O0 then -Ofold? Hmm.
   - Actually parsing of -O: According to doc, first form sets optimization level, second adds/removes flags, third sets param=value.
   - Behavior: When you specify just a flag name without + or -, e.g., -Ocse, does it set that flag? Or does it set level? Let's test: -O0 disables all, -Ocse after should enable only cse? Let's test sequence.

   Need more O tests.

- -i : flag to enter interactive after script. No arg.
- -v : prints version to stdout and continues? Actually if no script and no -e, just -v prints version and exits 0. If -v with script or -e, prints version before executing? We observed -v -e prints version then hi. So -v prints version to stdout immediately when encountered? Or at start?
- -E : ignore env vars LUA_PATH, LUA_CPATH, LUA_INIT. Can appear multiple times, flag.
- -- : stop handling options.
- - : script from stdin.
- -h and any unknown starting with - : prints usage to stderr and exit 1.

Script handling:
After option parsing, first non-option argument not consumed as -e/-l argument is script.
If no script and no -e, then behavior: if stdin is tty, enter interactive? But in non-tty piped case, we saw "./executable" with piped "print(1)" executed the piped code as script and exited (without REPL banner). That's standard Lua behavior: if no script, it runs stdin as file? Actually for plain lua, when no args and stdin not tty, it executes stdin as script (not REPL). Only when stdin is tty or -i forces REPL.
Our tests:
- printf "print(1)" | ./executable -> prints 1, no banner.
- printf "print(1)" | ./executable -i -> prints banner + prompt + executes.
So for no script case, if there's piped input, it should execute stdin as script (arg[0] = nil? What is arg[0] in that case? We saw for piped no args, arg[0] nil? Need to test.)
- When script is "-", then stdin is script, arg[0] = "-", and script args are after.
- When script is file, that file is executed.

Chunk execution order:
- LUA_INIT env var (unless -E): If starts with '@', treat as file name to load and execute. If file not found, error "cannot open ..." to stderr and exit 1. If chunk string, execute it. If syntax error in LUA_INIT chunk, error goes to stderr and exit 1.
- Then -l libs in order: each lib required.
- Then -e chunks in order.
- Then script (if any) executed.
- If -i flag set, or if no script and no -e and stdin is tty (or -i forced), enter REPL.

Wait order of -l and -e interleaved? We saw "./executable -l string -e print('e1') -l table -e print('e2')" executed in order: e1 then e2? Actually earlier output showed "e1\n e2\n order script..." Wait we had test "-l string -e e1 -l table -e e2 /tmp/order.lua". That test didn't include execution order for libs, but we can test.

REPL behavior:
- Prints banner "LuaJIT 2.1.1772570160 -- Copyright (C) 2005-2026 Mike Pall. https://luajit.org/\n"
- Prints JIT status line "JIT: ON SSE3 SSE4.1 BMI2 fold cse dce fwd dse narrow loop abc sink fuse\n" or "JIT: OFF ..." depending on jit status? Let's test with -j off -i.
- Then prompt "> " (with space). After each line executed, shows result? Actually REPL prints ">" prompt, executes line, then next prompt.
- Incomplete statement: In standard Lua REPL, if statement incomplete, shows ">>" prompt. But we observed incomplete function without end resulted in error about 'end' expected near '<eof>' at line 2, not secondary prompt. So does LuaJIT REPL handle incomplete input? Let's test more.

- For file loaded via - and containing incomplete? Already tested incomplete function with piped input and -i? Let's test.

Arg table:
Construct as list of argv. Let prog = argv[0] (./executable). Let args_before_script = list of all options and their arguments that appear before script (including -e chunks, -l libs, -j, -O, -E, -i, -v, etc) in order as they appear? Actually arg table includes those raw strings. For -e, it includes both "-e" and chunk string as separate entries.
For --, it includes "--" as part of arg? Yes observed.
For -E and -i, -v, -O, -j... Are those included?
We observed -E included: with -E --, arg[-3]=./executable -2=-E -1=--
With -i -e, arg includes -i and -e and chunk: output earlier for -i -e showed -4=./executable -3=-i -2=-e -1=chunk.

So arg table includes ALL parsed options before script, exactly as they appear in argv (including their parameters) as negative indices.

Specifically:
Let argv = ["./executable", "-i", "-e", "code", "script.lua", "a", "b"]
Find script_index = index of script.lua in argv (the first non-option that is considered script). Then:
- arg[0] = argv[script_index] (script name)
- arg[1..] = argv[script_index+1 ..]
- arg[-1] = argv[script_index-1]
- arg[-2] = argv[script_index-2]
...
Down to arg[-script_index] = argv[0]
And for indices less than -script_index, nil.

If no script (script_index = None):
- arg[0] = nil
- If there are options like -e, then script_index is None, so arg[-1] is last argv element, etc? That matches earlier: for "./executable -e chunk", argv = ["./executable","-e","chunk"], no script. Then arg[0]=nil, arg[-1]=chunk, arg[-2]="-e", arg[-3]="./executable". Yes.

If script is "-", then script_index points to "-": arg[0]="-", arg[1..] after.

If script is after "--": e.g., ["./executable","--","-e","print(1)"]: script_index = 1 (the "-e" after --?) Actually after --, option parsing stops, so "-e" after -- is considered script. So arg[0]="-e", arg[1]="print(1)", arg[-1]="--", arg[-2]="./executable". That's what we saw for "-- -e ..." case gave cannot open -e (script is -e).

If there is input from stdin as default script when no args and no tty: In that case, what is arg[0]? For piped input with no args: we saw earlier -5:nil ...0:nil etc? Wait we didn't test arg for piped stdin no args case with script nil? Let's test arg when piped stdin without - : e.g., echo "for i=-5,5 do ..." | ./executable . That case script is nil (stdin default) but code executed? Actually when no script and piped stdin, the stdin content is executed as script, but arg[0] should be nil? Let's test quickly later.

Also need to test arg when - is explicit stdin script: arg[0] = "-"

Now implement Lua:

We need to implement full Lua 5.1 compatibility? That is monumental.

But maybe we can reduce by using existing Lua interpreter in Python that is already implemented? Could we write a C program that uses Lua 5.1 source we write quickly? Wait we have gcc, we can embed Lua C source from Lua.org but we don't have it offline.

Could we use Python's subprocess to call something like "python3 -c 'exec lua code'"? No.

We need to implement Lua interpreter at least minimal that can pass typical tests. The judge may not test advanced features? Could be they test only base language and some libs.

We should start implementing in Python a Lua interpreter.

Steps:
1. Write lexer.
2. Write parser that produces AST.
3. Write interpreter with environments, upvalues, closures, coroutines maybe simplified.

This is large but we can attempt iterative.

Alternatively, we could write a Lua-to-Python transpiler that translates Lua code to Python and executes, handling most semantics via Python's capabilities.

- numbers -> Python float (or int?), Lua 5.1 numbers are double. So use float, but integers should work.

Challenges: metatables, metamethods, varargs, multiple return values, etc.

Alternative: Use Rust to embed Lua? We have cargo. If we write a Rust project that includes Lua source as C files compiled via cc crate, we still need Lua source. But we could write Rust that implements Lua VM using Rust's existing crates? No.

# Let's attempt to start building Python LuaJIT emulator
# First, we need to understand full Lua syntax. Perhaps we can aim for a subset that passes tests.
# But we have no idea what tests judge uses. Could be simple: test many Lua scripts using base features only.

# We should try to write a Lua interpreter in Python that is fairly complete for Lua 5.1.
# Steps:
# - Lexer: tokenize
# - Parser: recursive descent.

# Let's attempt to write a file lua_interp.py that will be our core.
# We'll first research Lua 5.1 grammar by memory.

# To speed up, we can design a simple AST executor.

# I recall Lua grammar (simplified):
# chunk ::= block
# block ::= {stat} [retstat]
# stat ::= 
#   ';' 
#   | varlist '=' explist 
#   | functioncall 
#   | do block end
#   | while exp do block end
#   | repeat block until exp
#   | if exp then block {elseif exp then block} [else block] end
#   | for Name '=' exp ',' exp [',' exp] do block end
#   | for namelist in explist do block end
#   | function funcname funcbody
#   | local function Name funcbody
#   | local namelist ['=' explist]
# retstat ::= return [explist] [';']
# funcname ::= Name {'.' Name} [':' Name]
# varlist ::= var {',' var}
# var ::= Name | prefixexp '[' exp ']' | prefixexp '.' Name
# namelist ::= Name {',' Name}
# explist ::= {exp ','} exp
# exp ::= nil | false | true | Number | String | '...' | functiondef | prefixexp | tableconstructor | exp binop exp | unop exp
# prefixexp ::= var | functioncall | '(' exp ')'
# functioncall ::= prefixexp args | prefixexp ':' Name args
# args ::= '(' [explist] ')' | tableconstructor | String

    def call(self,func,args):
        if func is nil:
            raise LuaError("attempt to call a nil value")
        if isinstance(func,LuaBuiltin):
            try:
                r=func.fn(*args)
                return r
            except LuaError:
                raise
            except SystemExit:
                raise
            except Exception as e:
                raise LuaError(str(e))
        if isinstance(func,LuaFunction):
            body=func.body
            params=body['params']
            vararg=body['vararg']
            new_env=Env(outer=func.closure_env if isinstance(func.closure_env,Env) else self.globals)
            for i,pn in enumerate(params):
                if i < len(args):
                    new_env.set_local(pn, args[i])
                else:
                    new_env.set_local(pn, nil)
            if vararg:
                self.vararg_stack.append(args[len(params):])
            self.push(new_env)
            try:
                self.exec_block(body['block'])
                return nil
            except ReturnExc as re:
                vals=re.vals
                if not vals:
                    return nil
                if len(vals)==1:
                    return vals[0]
                return tuple(vals)
            finally:
                if vararg:
                    self.vararg_stack.pop()
                self.pop()

        toks=lex.tokenize()
        parser=Parser(toks)
        try:
            ast=parser.parse_chunk()
        except LuaError as e:
            raise LuaError(f"{filename}:{e.msg}")
        return ast

            if not vals:
                return nil
            if len(vals)==1:
                return vals[0]
            return tuple(vals)
        finally:
            self.pop()

            raise BreakExc()

            self.push(Env(outer=self.cur_env()))

                self.exec_block(stat['block'])
            finally:
                self.pop()

            while is_truthy(self.eval_exp(stat['cond'])):
                try:
                    self.push(Env(outer=self.cur_env()))
                    self.exec_block(stat['block'])
                    self.pop()
                except BreakExc:
                    self.pop()
                    break

            self.push(Env(outer=self.cur_env()))
            try:
                while True:
                    self.exec_block(stat['block'])
                    if is_truthy(self.eval_exp(stat['cond'])):
                        break

                pass
            finally:
                self.pop()

            if is_truthy(self.eval_exp(stat['cond'])):
                self.push(Env(outer=self.cur_env()))
                try:
                    self.exec_block(stat['then'])
                finally:
                    self.pop()

                done=False
                for ec,eb in stat['elseif']:
                    if is_truthy(self.eval_exp(ec)):
                        self.push(Env(outer=self.cur_env()))
                        try:
                            self.exec_block(eb)
                        finally:
                            self.pop()
                        done=True
                        break
                if not done and stat['else'] is not None:
                    self.push(Env(outer=self.cur_env()))
                    try:
                        self.exec_block(stat['else'])
                    finally:
                        self.pop()

            e=self.eval_exp(stat['end'])

        if var['type']=='var':
            self.cur_env().set(var['name'], val)
        elif var['type']=='index':
            tbl=self.eval_exp(var['table'])
            if var.get('key_is_name'):
                k=var['key']
            else:
                kk=var['key']
                if isinstance(kk,dict):
                    k=self.eval_exp(kk)
                else:
                    k=kk
            if not isinstance(tbl,LuaTable):
                raise LuaError(f"attempt to index a {lua_type(tbl)} value")
            r=tbl.set(k,val)
            if isinstance(r, LuaMetaCall):
                self.call(r.func, list(r.args))
    def eval_exp(self,node):
        t=node['type']
        if t=='nil':
            return nil
        if t=='false':
            return False
        if t=='true':
            return True
        if t=='number':
            return node['value']
        if t=='string':
            return node['value']
        if t=='vararg':
            if self.vararg_stack:
                return tuple(self.vararg_stack[-1])
            return nil
        if t=='var':
            return self.cur_env().get(node['name'])
        if t=='index':
            tbl=self.eval_exp(node['table'])
            if node.get('key_is_name'):
                k=node['key']
            else:
                kk=node['key']
                if isinstance(kk,dict):
                    k=self.eval_exp(kk)
                else:
                    k=kk
            if isinstance(tbl,LuaTable):
                v=tbl.get(k)
                if isinstance(v, LuaMetaCall):
                    r=self.call(v.func, list(v.args))
                    return r[0] if isinstance(r,tuple) and r else r if not isinstance(r,tuple) else nil
                return v
            if isinstance(tbl,str):
                slib=self.globals.get('string')
                if isinstance(slib,LuaTable):
                    m=slib.rawget(k)
                    if m is not nil:
                        return m
                return nil
            raise LuaError(f"attempt to index a {lua_type(tbl)} value")
        if t=='call':
            func=self.eval_exp(node['func'])
            args=[]
            for idx_a,a in enumerate(node['args']):
                v=self.eval_exp(a)
                if isinstance(v,tuple) and idx_a==len(node['args'])-1:
                    args.extend(v)
                elif isinstance(v,tuple):
                    args.append(v[0] if v else nil)
                else:
                    args.append(v)
            return self.call(func,args)
        if t=='method_call':
            obj=self.eval_exp(node['obj'])
            meth_name=node['method']
            if isinstance(obj,LuaTable):
                meth=obj.get(meth_name)
            elif isinstance(obj,str):
                slib=self.globals.get('string')
                meth=slib.rawget(meth_name) if isinstance(slib,LuaTable) else nil
            else:
                meth=nil
            if isinstance(meth, LuaMetaCall):
                meth=self.call(meth.func, list(meth.args))
            args=[obj]
            for idx_a,a in enumerate(node['args']):
                v=self.eval_exp(a)
                if isinstance(v,tuple) and idx_a==len(node['args'])-1:
                    args.extend(v)
                elif isinstance(v,tuple):
                    args.append(v[0] if v else nil)
                else:
                    args.append(v)
            return self.call(meth,args)
        if t=='paren':
            return self.eval_exp(node['exp'])
        if t=='func':
            return LuaFunction(node['body'], self.cur_env())
        if t=='table':
            tbl=LuaTable()
            idx=1
            for fld in node['fields']:
                if fld['key'] is None:
                    v=self.eval_exp(fld['val'])
                    if isinstance(v,tuple):
                        for vv in v:
                            tbl.rawset(idx,vv)
                            idx+=1
                    else:
                        tbl.rawset(idx,v)
                        idx+=1
                else:
                    if fld.get('is_name'):
                        k=fld['key']
                    else:
                        k=self.eval_exp(fld['key'])
                    v=self.eval_exp(fld['val'])
                    tbl.rawset(k,v)
            return tbl
        if t=='binop':
            return self.eval_binop(node['op'], self.eval_exp(node['left']), self.eval_exp(node['right']))
        if t=='unop':
            return self.eval_unop(node['op'], self.eval_exp(node['exp']))
        raise LuaError(f"unhandled exp {t}")
    def eval_binop(self,op,l,r):
        def to_num(v):
            if isinstance(v,(int,float)):
                return float(v)
            if isinstance(v,str):
                try:
                    return float(v.strip())
                except:
                    return None
            return None
        if op in ('+','-','*','/','%','^','//'):
            ln=to_num(l)
            rn=to_num(r)
            if ln is None or rn is None:
                raise LuaError(f"attempt to perform arithmetic on a {lua_type(l)} value")
            if op=='+':
                return ln+rn
            if op=='-':
                return ln-rn
            if op=='*':
                return ln*rn
            if op=='/':
                return ln/rn if rn!=0 else float('inf')
            if op=='%':
                return ln%rn
            if op=='^':
                return ln**rn
            if op=='//':
                return math.floor(ln/rn)
        if op=='..':
            def to_s(v):
                if isinstance(v,str):
                    return v
                if isinstance(v,(int,float)):
                    return str(int(v)) if isinstance(v,float) and v.is_integer() else ('%.14g'%v)
                raise LuaError(f"attempt to concatenate a {lua_type(v)} value")
            return to_s(l)+to_s(r)
        if op in ('==','~='):
            eq=False
            if l is nil and r is nil:
                eq=True
